title: The one retention channel most businesses near 100k underuse
hook: The most valuable two weeks in a 100k business are the two weeks after the customer buys.
caption:
The most valuable two weeks in a 100k business are the two weeks after the customer buys.

Most owners treat this window like a formality. One welcome email, then silence. The next message lands when there is a promotion, a product update, or a renewal.

That is a missed window. A customer who just paid you is the most open to hearing from you they will ever be. The second purchase, the referral, the review, the habit, all of it starts here, and all of it fades week by week after.

Three things that fit inside those two weeks.

1. A short email on the day they buy, from a real person, that welcomes them and tells them what to expect. Not a tutorial. A greeting.

2. A check-in near day three or four. A simple question. What are you trying to do with this? Not a survey. A sentence.

3. A follow-up in the second week pointing them at the second thing your product or service can do for them. Not an upsell. A useful next step.

You do not need a clever sequence. You need presence in the window that matters most.

title: How I rebuilt Passion.io's retention system: what I actually did
hook: How we lifted revenue per lead from $13 to $27 [verify with Muddassir] for a Passion.io client. Same list. Same product. Better use of what they already had.
tweets:
How we lifted revenue per lead from $13 to $27 [verify with Muddassir: final numbers, timeframe] for a Passion.io client in the online creator space.

No new traffic. Same list. Same product. Better use of the list they already had.

Thread on what moved.

Where we started.

Standard broadcasts going to everyone on the list on the same day. Open rates looked fine. Revenue was flat. The list was being shouted at, not written to.

First move. Split the list into three groups based on behaviour, not size.

Group A bought in the last three months.
Group B bought six to eighteen months ago and had gone quiet.
Group C had never bought but still opened emails.

Group A is the easiest group to underpay attention to, because they already pay you.

We sent them an early access email twenty-four hours before anything public. It read as a thank-you, not a promotion. Revenue from this group doubled first.

Group B needed a specific reason to come back. Not "we miss you."

A new product that matched something they bought before. One sentence. One link. It brought back a real slice of the group.

Group C needed the cleanest offer. One hook. One clear saving. Four emails through the window with rising urgency.

Accept that some of this group never buys and write for the ones who will.

Send times mattered more than subject lines.

Each group got a different send time that matched when their past opens had landed. No clever trick. Just reading what the data already said.

Result. Revenue per lead almost doubled over the window [verify with Muddassir: exact figure].

Most of the lift came from Group A, at the smallest send volume. The list we had was bigger than we were treating it.

The move most businesses can copy this week.

Pull your list. Split by last purchase date. Write one different email to each group. Send at different times. That is the whole project.

title: Why email is still the highest ROI channel for retention
hook: "Email is dead" is a line people use to avoid building the one channel they actually own.
caption:
"Email is dead" is a line people use to avoid building the one channel they actually own.

An inbox does not change its rules on you next week. It does not throttle a post because the first twenty likes were slow. It shows up the same way on a Tuesday as it does on a Sunday.

That is the channel most businesses near 100k are not writing for.

title: LI Second Post: Welcome sequence fundamentals
hook: How to write the emails a new customer reads in the first week.
caption:
How to write the emails a new customer reads in the first week.

The first seven days after somebody buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them. Four emails is usually enough.

Day 0. Short. From a person. Let them know what kind of business they have joined and what to expect from you over the next week.

Day 1. Point them at one small win they can get with the product or service today. Not a full tour. One thing done.

Day 3. Ask a question. "What are you trying to get done with this?" One line back from them is worth more than any survey.

Day 7. Suggest a standing time or a second use case. Something that turns a purchase into a habit.

Four emails, one week. Rewrite yours if you have not in a year.

title: How to do cold outreach as a creative strategist and stand out
hook: Why cold outreach is still worth your time, even in 2026.
caption:
Why cold outreach is still worth your time, even in 2026.

Here is how I think about it. In my first year online I ran more than twenty million cold emails [verify with Muddassir: exact figure]. That is why I never needed to build a big audience first. Never starved for leads. Never slid into DMs for "networking."

Most people today will tell you cold outreach hurts your brand. My take is the opposite. If a creative strategist needs cold outreach, it usually means they do not have budget for anything else, no leverage in the market yet, and no real brand built. A brand that does not exist cannot be hurt.

Done right, cold outreach is a volume game. If you cannot play volume, do not attempt it. If you can, it is the fastest way to prove to yourself that you can start and hold a conversation with a stranger. That skill does not go away.

What cold outreach built for me.

Hundreds of booked calls a month in that first year. Hundreds of tests on a single sentence. A rapport with strangers that let me ask for high-ticket work on the first call, because the first impression was never "please hire me." It was "here is what I see in your business."

What I would tell a creative strategist starting today. If you can run Facebook ads for yourself, that is probably a cleaner road to the same outcome. If you cannot, run cold outreach. Send messages that are not pitches. Send a piece of thinking about their business. No rate. No ask. No services page.

Ten sent properly gets a handful of replies. A handful of replies gets a paid conversation.

title: The outreach DM most creative strategists keep sending (and what to send instead)
hook: Your prospect reads that exact DM forty times a day.
caption:
Your prospect reads that exact DM forty times a day. "Hey, I noticed your website could use some work" has been the opening line of outreach for the last five years. The prospect is numb to it.

Send a piece of thinking instead. Screenshot one of their ads. Three sentences on what you would test next. No rate. No ask. No services page. Just the thinking.

title: Bad DM vs good DM, side by side
hook: Flattery is not personalization. Prospects can tell the difference in three seconds.
caption:
Flattery is not personalization. Prospects can tell the difference in three seconds.

One is flattery. "Love your content." The other is observation. "Your Q4 ad is fading, here is what I would test next."

If you are sending cold outreach as a creative strategist, send the second one. Always.
